BA Stock Edges Lower As Boeing Reportedly Trims 5% Of Commercial Airplanes Workforce
sum: Shares of Boeing Co (BA) slipped about 1% on Monday following reports that the company is making fresh workforce reductions tied to a slower-than-expected production recovery in its commercial airplanes unit.

According to a report from CNBC, Boeing said it will reduce the commercial airplane workforce by about 5% through a combination of attrition and involuntary layoffs, with notifications beginning in December. Stephanie Pope, head of the commercial aircraft unit, reportedly told employees in a memo that revised production schedules and lower aircraft output have left the division overstaffed relative to its updated business plan. The company is still working to stabilize rates on the 737 Max, its best-selling model.

CEO Kelly Ortberg indicated late last month that significant ramp-up of 737 Max output is now not expected until the second half of 2027—later than previously projected. Boeing has been working to stabilize production at 47 Max aircraft per month and is targeting 52 per month only in the second half of 2027, the CEO said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. The commercial division employed about 50,500 people as of the end of 2025, implying that the workforce reduction will impact about 2,500 employees.

The cuts come against a backdrop of persistent losses in the commercial airplanes business. In the third quarter of 2026, the unit generated roughly $10.7 billion in revenue but posted an operating loss of $697 million. The division delivered 161 aircraft during the quarter. Higher supply-chain costs, a less favorable mix of deliveries, and elevated expenses weighed on results, even as overall company losses narrowed sharply from the prior year.

Boeing has already pushed back its timeline for reaching a stable 47-per-month 737 rate into early 2027, missing earlier internal targets and its 2026 delivery goals. Free-cash-flow expectations have also been tempered, with management guiding to roughly $3 billion in 2027—below prior analyst consensus.

However, the FAA certified the smallest 737-7 variant in August and the largest 737-10 in October, completing type certification for the main 737 MAX family after multi-year delays and clearing the way for deliveries.

Boeing's underlying equity has faced volatility tied to production schedules, delivery targets, and regulatory developments. Tokenized stock traders may have reacted to company-specific news that did not affect the broader tokenized equity complex.

Boeing (BA) stock fell 26.4% from August 7 to November 5, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 5.0%. The price appears to want a steadier 737 factory, and management said on October 27 that it does not expect steady output at 47 jets a month until 2027. Yet management credited third-quarter sales growth mainly to defense and services, not jetliners. That is the mismatch, though defense helps only if it keeps growing at a real profit. So how fast is Boeing’s defense business growing?

Defense revenue rose 15% to $7.9 billion in the third quarter of 2026, while Boeing’s jetliner sales shrank. Over the same quarter, revenue from its jetliners fell 3% to $10.7 billion. Management attributed that decline to a less favorable mix of deliveries. That makes defense about a third of Boeing’s $24.2 billion in quarterly sales.

Management credited the defense rise mainly to higher volume, including classified missile and weapons programs. It said about 2 points of the increase came from Spirit, which contributed about $150 million of the unit’s sales in the quarter. Orders are running well ahead of sales. The defense unit booked $23 billion of orders in the quarter, and management put its backlog at a record $101 billion. That backlog does not yet include the US Navy’s next fighter jet, which the Navy selected Boeing to design, build and deliver.

Management also expects more defense growth than it did a year ago, forecasting revenue growth in the middle single digits or higher going forward, compared with the low single digits it was thinking of then. That is still slower than the third quarter’s 15%, about 2 points of which came from Spirit.

Not yet. On management’s own measure, the defense unit’s operating margin was 6.2% in the third quarter, and that figure includes a $252 million gain on the sale of HRL Laboratories. That gain accounted for about half the unit’s operating profit; without it, the margin would have been about 3%. Management said it remains confident of reaching high single-digit margins, so the profit is still catching up with the sales.
That matters because the jetliners are where Boeing loses money. On the same measure, the jetliner unit’s operating margin was negative 6.5%.

Boeing, ServiceNow and Nebius Keep Their Stock Off ICE-OKX Token Venue, Lifting Objectors to 62
sum: About 62 companies have now objected to tokenized trading of their shares on OKXICE TSV, the planned onchain stock venue owned by Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and OKX, according to a public notice the venue dated Nov. 4. The newest names on the list are Boeing, ServiceNow and Nebius Group.

They follow Apple, The Home Depot and GE Vernova, whose objections first appeared in the venue’s Nov. 3 notice, when Unchained counted 59 objectors. By Unchained’s count of the venue’s filings, the list stood at 56 on Nov. 2 and at nine in mid-October. No company has come off it. The Nov. 4 notice gives no reasons for any objection.

Lumida Wealth founder Ram Ahluwalia offered one explanation when he spoke on Unchained’s Bits + Bips on Nov. 2. “The issuers like to control their stock. They know their buyer base. They know who their beneficial owners are,” he said. On the same episode, he said firms whose businesses touch the trade have their own reasons: “If you’re Goldman Sachs, you’re providing financing on these assets, you’re supposed to object.” Goldman Sachs is on the venue’s list.

The Securities and Exchange Commission’s exemptive order for tokenized securities venues, dated Sept. 17, sets the rules. Before a venue lists a token of a company’s stock created by an unaffiliated third party, it must send that company written notice, and trading cannot start for at least 30 calendar days after the company receives it. A written objection inside that window keeps the token off the venue, which then has five business days to publish a revised notice.
The order lists concerns an issuer might weigh, including “the risk of maintaining its shareholder register related to onchain transfers” and possible effects on the price of the underlying stock.
Andrew Cuomo, who co-chairs the joint venture, said on a press call with reporters on Oct. 29 that “you’ll have a lot of companies that take the position I want to wait and see.”

OKXICE LLC, a Texas company owned 50% by ICE and 50% by OKC USA Holding Inc., runs the venue. Tokenized stocks are set to trade against supported payment stablecoins in permissioned Uniswap v4 pools on XLayer, open only to wallets that hold a soulbound token the venue issues.

Shares of Boeing (BA) have declined 27.8% over the past three months, compared with a 1.7% drop for the S&P 500. The stock took its biggest hit on October 27, falling 10.7% on the day of its third-quarter report. With management pointing to a record $745 billion backlog, you might assume most of the risk is already out of the shares. So how has Boeing stock held up when the whole market sold off?

Boeing shares have declined an average of 23.6% across 15 market shocks since 2007, compared with a 15.8% drop for the S&P 500 over those same windows. The stock recorded its steepest loss during the COVID-19 shock of 2020, falling 72% alongside a 34% drop for the broader index. During the 2008-2009 Global Financial Crisis, Boeing shares fell 66%, against 53% for the S&P 500.

Recovering from these lows has also taken time. The median rebound from a shock low required 8.1 months, though three recoveries lasted more than a year, including 48.1 months following the 2008-2009 crisis. The stock has not returned to its level prior to the 2020 shock, and its latest close is 48.8% below its February 2020 peak.

Boeing generated $94.9 billion in revenue over the twelve months to September 2026, a 17.5% increase. The company still posted a $165 million operating loss, although that was much smaller than the $8.4 billion operating loss reported a year earlier. While Boeing reported a net profit for the twelve months, a single quarter, the three months to December 2025, produced an $8.22 billion net profit on an $815 million operating loss. That single quarter generated a larger profit than the $7.66 billion net profit for the entire twelve months, so the other three quarters together lost money.

The company also carries more debt relative to its size than the broader S&P 500, with debt equaling 33.4% of its market value compared with 19.2% for the index. Over their latest twelve months, peers RTX and Lockheed Martin each achieved an operating margin of 11.8%, while Boeing’s operating margin sat close to zero.
On the October 27 call, management said that establishing a fully stable 737 production rate of 47 jets a month is taking longer than expected and will run into 2027.

The biggest risk has not really changed. Recent results and contract wins support demand visibility, but they do not yet resolve execution, cash flow, or balance sheet pressure.

The clearest recent development tied to the current story is FAA certification of the 737 10. This removes a key regulatory overhang and completes the 737 MAX family. That directly connects to Boeing's record commercial backlog and gives the business a path to start delivering a high capacity, high seat count variant that already represents a large share of unfilled MAX orders.

Management has pointed to long-standing supply chain architecture as a primary factor dictating how margins are distributed between airframers and component suppliers on current delivery programs. Boeing is managing supplier bottlenecks on 787 engine deliveries, which lagged in the first half of 2026 and constrain the ramp from eight to ten aircraft per month. Commercial Airplanes still lost money on operations in the June 2026 quarter despite handing over 171 airplanes, its most since 2018, though its margin improved from a year earlier on the higher volume.

The CFO says program cash margins on the 737 and 787 sit only slightly above breakeven, held down largely by a pricing drag that fades as deliveries climb and better-priced backlog comes through. The 737 is ramping to 47 airplanes per month. Volume is arriving before the margin does.

items.t: NASA May X Out Boeing's SLS Rocket Ship From Future Moon Landings
sum: Once upon a time, NASA's moon ambitions promised to pave a Milky Way to profits for Boeing (BA +0.97%). Collaborating with fellow big space companies, including Lockheed Martin (LMT +1.90%) and Northrop Grumman (NOC +1.28%), to launch as many as 20 Space Launch System megarockets to the moon at $4.1 billion a pop, Boeing stood in line to share in some $82 billion in revenue across 20 missions under NASA's Project Artemis.

As Bloomberg reported last week, NASA is revising plans for future moon missions. Instead of paying Boeing to launch an SLS rocket to propel a Lockheed Martin Orion spacecraft into lunar orbit -- there to dock with a SpaceX Human Landing System (HLS) for landing -- NASA now sees a simpler way to get astronauts from Earth to the moon.

The existing framework -- SLS launching Orions, Orions docking with HLSes near the moon, and so on -- will still be used for the Artemis IV and V moon landings taking place in 2028 and 2029. But beginning with Artemis VI, the plan will be to launch Orion atop a smaller rocket and have Orion dock with HLS in Earth orbit. Orion and HLS will then travel in tandem to the moon, with HLS providing the propulsion. There, astronauts will transfer from Orion to HLS, descend to the moon, ascend from the moon, redock, and retransfer.

The advantage of this new approach is Orion won't be traveling as far under its own power, it won't need a rocket as big (or expensive) as SLS to give it an initial boost. A smaller Vulcan Centaur rocket (built 50-50 by Boeing and Lockheed) might not be able to send Orion all the way to the moon, but should suffice to put Orion in Earth orbit, at which point HLS could take over.
So could a SpaceX Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, or a New Glenn rocket from Blue Origin.

Of course, the disadvantage from Boeing's perspective is that, instead of charging NASA $3 billion (roughly SLS' share of an Artemis mission cost) for each launch, it will only be able to charge a smaller fee for a Vulcan launch -- on the order of $110 million. And it will only get even that much if SpaceX or Blue Origin doesn't offer to do the launch for cheaper.
Pick your poison. Either option means less money for Boeing, and much less than $82 billion for the entire Artemis project.

sum: Boeing BA delivered 117 737 and 27 787 jets in the fourth quarter of 2025, up 225% and 80%, respectively, since 2024. Why it matters: We estimate that half of Boeing’s enterprise value is derived from its 737 product line. Increasing the rate at which the company can make and deliver these jets is the single biggest driver of near- and long-term profitability and cash flow, and Boeing received FAA approval to do so in October 2025.

- Boeing has designed four versions of its newest generation of 737 jets. The 737 MAX 8 and 737 MAX 9 entered service by 2018, but its shorter 737 MAX 7 and stretched 737 MAX 10 have had their flight certification delayed by the FAA because new materials and temperature tolerances in their engine nacelles complicate deicing.

- Our forecast for 2026 deliveries of 737s (including shipping previously built ones from inventory) is 117 more jets than the 447 the company achieved in 2025, and we estimate the company may deliver 38 more 787s than it did last year. Both should be positive developments for the company’s turnaround trajectory.
The bottom line: Our fair value estimate for wide-moat Boeing remains $246 per share. The shares trade very close to our current fair value estimate.

Coming up: We’ll eagerly monitor Boeing’s progress on its 737 and 787 deliveries, as well as flight testing and certification of its newest and largest jet, the 777X, due later in 2026. Here’s Why Boeing Outpaced The Stock Market Despite A Year Of Delays
sum: US-based aerospace manufacturer Boeing had a fundamentally bizarre 2025. On the industrial side, the year was still defined primarily by flight constraints, including tight FAA oversight, delivery bottlenecks, and the slow grind of rebuilding quality discipline after years of crises. The clearest symbol of that hangover was the 777X, where Boeing again pushed the first delivery of the type to 2027 and took about a $5 billion program charge as a result. One would expect these kinds of headlines to financially punish cyclical manufacturers. Despite these extensive and well-documented production challenges (which follow on the heels of a reputational hit), the market treated Boeing more like a turnaround candidate than a market laggard.

Bullish investors have increasingly framed 2025 as a bridge year for the manufacturer, supporting delivery and cash-flow recovery. Boeing's narrowbody engine production steadied as 737 MAX production reached 38 per month in the second quarter, and the FAA later cleared the company to increase the aircraft's output to 42 per month. This all comes as 787 Dreamliner deliveries continue to rebuild. With a massive outstanding backlog, the equity valuation story became less about whether demand exists and more about Boeing's ability to execute given its extensive challenges. In December, Boeing's CFO said he expects higher deliveries of 737 and 787 aircraft next year to support a return to positive free cash flow in 2026. This forward arc is what we aim to unpack in this analysis. As Boeing's valuation continues to rise, we keep in mind the ongoing certification challenges that compound and the supply chain difficulties that have only begun to ease.

Boeing's 2025 stock performance looks like a classic rerating. The carrier had previously been trading at a survival discount and has been rerated towards an execution-oriented positive outlook. Boeing shares closed at $171 last January and have since risen above $218, highlighting gains of more than 22%, all during a year when the company faced reputation struggles and analyst downgrades. Throughout the same window, the S&P 500's year-to-date return was around 18%.

items.t: Trump buys millions in Boeing bonds while awarding it contracts
sum: Trump bought up to $6 million worth of corporate bonds in Boeing, even as the Defense Department has awarded the company multi-billion dollar contracts, new financial disclosures reveal.

According to the documents, Trump bought between $1 million and $5 million worth of Boeing bonds on August 28. On September 19, he bought more Boeing bonds worth between $500,000 and $1 million. In total, Trump appears to have bought at least $185 million worth of corporate and municipal bonds since the start of his presidency.

Kedric Payne, Vice President of the Campaign Legal Center, told RS in a phone interview there is “absolutely” a conflict of interest in Trump’s purchase of Boeing, especially since it is “a government contractor that is connected to military actions that the president controls almost unilaterally.”

Trump also bought between $1 and $5 million worth of Intel bonds in August, a week after the Trump administration took a 10% stake in the company. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted on Truth Social on August 25. Trump purchased Intel bonds on August 29.

The partial purchase of the chip manufacturer, done under the auspices of driving technology research vital to national security, drew praise from some advocates of corporate accountability, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

Others raised concerns about how the U.S. government could maintain fairness. “Will the government favor firms in which it owns stakes over other competitors that might have better technology or processes?” asked Peter Harrell, a Non Resident Fellow at the Carnegie Endowment. Since the U.S. government’s partial ownership could give the Trump administration far more influence over the company, Trump’s personal investment in Intel could blur the lines between personal, corporate, and national interests. Intel has said the government’s partial ownership would be passive, with the government agreeing to “vote with the company’s Board of Directors on matters requiring shareholder approval, with limited exceptions.”

Upon entering office, Trump did not move his assets into a blind trust run by an independent trustee that could not be directed by the Trump family. Instead, he opted to hand over his business empire to his sons.
